{{Short description|Class of compact connected topological spaces}}
:''This page discusses a class of topological groups. For the wrapped loop of wire, see [[Solenoid]].''

{{Group theory sidebar |Topological}}
[[File:Smale-Williams Solenoid Large.png|thumb|right|300px|The Smale-Williams solenoid.]]
In [[mathematics]], a '''solenoid''' is a [[compact space|compact]] [[connected space|connected]] [[topological space]] (i.e. a [[continuum (topology)|continuum]]) that may be obtained as the [[inverse limit]] of an inverse system of [[topological group]]s and [[continuous function|continuous]] [[homomorphism]]s

:<math>f_i: S_{i+1} \to S_i \quad \forall i \ge 0</math>

where each <math>S_i</math> is a [[circle]] and ''f''<sub>''i''</sub> is the map that uniformly wraps the circle <math>S_{i+1}</math> for <math>n_{i+1}</math> times (<math>n_{i+1} \geq 2</math>) around the circle <math>S_i</math>.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Hewitt |first1=Edwin |last2=Ross |first2=Kenneth A.|title=Abstract Harmonic Analysis I: Structure of Topological Groups Integration Theory Group Representations | location = Berlin-New York | publisher = Springer|date=1979 |series=Grundlehren der Mathematischen Wissenschaften|volume=115|doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-8638-2|isbn=978-0-387-94190-5 }}</ref>{{rp|Ch. 2 Def. (10.12)}}
This construction can be carried out geometrically in the three-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] '''R'''<sup>3</sup>. A solenoid is a one-dimensional homogeneous [[indecomposable continuum]] that has the structure of an [[Abelian group|abelian]] compact [[topological group]].

Solenoids were first introduced by [[Leopold Vietoris|Vietoris]] for the <math>n_i = 2</math> case,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vietoris |first=L. |date=December 1927 |title=Über den höheren Zusammenhang kompakter Räume und eine Klasse von zusammenhangstreuen Abbildungen |url=http://dx.doi.org/10.1007/bf01447877 |journal=Mathematische Annalen |volume=97 |issue=1 |pages=454–472 |doi=10.1007/bf01447877 |s2cid=121172198 |issn=0025-5831|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and by [[David van Dantzig|van Dantzig]] the <math>n_i = n</math> case, where <math>n\geq 2</math> is fixed.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=van Dantzig |first=D. |date=1930 |title=Ueber topologisch homogene Kontinua |journal=Fundamenta Mathematicae |volume=15 |pages=102–125 |doi=10.4064/fm-15-1-102-125 |issn=0016-2736|doi-access=free }}</ref> Such a solenoid arises as a one-dimensional '''expanding attractor''', or '''Smale–Williams attractor''', and forms an important example in the theory of [[hyperbolic dynamics|hyperbolic]] [[dynamical system]]s.

== Construction ==

=== Geometric construction and the Smale–Williams attractor ===
[[File:Smale-Williams Solenoid.png|thumb|300px|A solid torus wrapped twice around inside another solid torus in '''R'''<sup>3</sup>]]
[[File:Solenoid.gif|thumb|300px|The first six steps in the construction of the Smale-Williams attractor.]]
Each solenoid may be constructed as the intersection of a nested system of embedded solid tori in '''R'''<sup>3</sup>.

Fix a sequence of natural numbers {''n''<sub>''i''</sub>}, ''n''<sub>''i''</sub> &ge; 2. Let ''T''<sub>0</sub> = ''S''<sup>1</sup> &times; ''D'' be a [[solid torus]]. For each ''i'' &ge; 0, choose a solid torus ''T''<sub>''i''+1</sub> that is wrapped longitudinally ''n''<sub>''i''</sub> times inside the solid torus ''T''<sub>''i''</sub>. Then their intersection

: <math>\Lambda=\bigcap_{i\ge 0}T_i</math>

is [[homeomorphic]] to the solenoid constructed as the inverse limit of the system of circles with the maps determined by the sequence {''n''<sub>''i''</sub>}.

Here is a variant of this construction isolated by [[Stephen Smale]] as an example of an '''expanding attractor''' in the theory of smooth dynamical systems. Denote the angular coordinate on the circle ''S''<sup>1</sup> by ''t'' (it is defined mod 2&pi;) and consider the complex coordinate ''z'' on the two-dimensional [[unit disk]] ''D''. Let ''f'' be the map of the solid torus ''T'' = ''S''<sup>1</sup> &times; ''D'' into itself given by the explicit formula

: <math> f(t,z) = \left(2t, \tfrac{1}{4}z + \tfrac{1}{2}e^{it}\right).</math>

This map is a smooth [[embedding]] of ''T'' into itself that preserves the [[foliation]] by meridional disks (the constants 1/2 and 1/4 are somewhat arbitrary, but it is essential that 1/4 < 1/2 and 1/4 + 1/2 < 1). If ''T'' is imagined as a rubber tube, the map ''f'' stretches it in the longitudinal direction, contracts each meridional disk, and wraps the deformed tube twice inside ''T'' with twisting, but without self-intersections. The [[hyperbolic set]] ''&Lambda;'' of the discrete dynamical system (''T'', ''f'') is the intersection of the sequence of nested solid tori described above, where ''T''<sub>''i''</sub> is the image of ''T'' under the ''i''th iteration of the map ''f''. This set is a one-dimensional (in the sense of [[topological dimension]]) [[attractor]], and the dynamics of ''f'' on ''&Lambda;'' has the following interesting properties:

* meridional disks are the [[stable manifold]]s, each of which intersects ''&Lambda;'' over a [[Cantor set]]
* [[periodic point]]s of ''f'' are [[dense subset|dense]] in ''&Lambda;''
* the map ''f'' is [[topologically transitive]] on ''&Lambda;''

General theory of solenoids and expanding attractors, not necessarily one-dimensional, was developed by R. F. Williams and involves a projective system of infinitely many copies of a compact [[branched manifold]] in place of the circle, together with an expanding self-[[immersion (mathematics)|immersion]].

=== Construction in toroidal coordinates ===
In the [[Toroidal and poloidal coordinates|toroidal coordinates]] with radius <math>R</math>, the solenoid can be parametrized by <math>t\in \R</math> as<math display="block">\zeta = 2\pi t, \quad re^{i\theta} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty r_k e^{2\pi i \omega_k t}</math>where

<math>\omega_k = \frac{1}{n_1 \cdots n_k}, \quad r_k = R \delta_1 \cdots \delta_k</math>

Here, <math>\delta_k</math> are adjustable shape-parameters, with constraint <math>0 < \delta < 1 - \frac{1}{1 + \sin \frac{\pi}{n_k}}</math>. In particular, <math>\delta = \frac{1}{2n_k}</math> works.

Let <math>S\subset \R^3</math> be the solenoid constructed this way, then the topology of the solenoid is just the subset topology induced by the [[Euclidean topology]] on <math>\R^3</math>.

Since the parametrization is bijective, we can pullback the topology on <math>S</math> to <math>\R</math>, which makes <math>\R</math> itself the solenoid. This allows us to construct the inverse limit maps explicitly:<math display="block">g_k: \R \to S_k, \quad g_k(t) = (r, \theta, \zeta)\text{ in toroidal coordinates, where } \zeta = 2\pi t, \quad re^{i\theta} = \sum_{k=1}^k r_k e^{2\pi i \omega_k t} </math>

=== Construction by symbolic dynamics ===
Viewed as a set, the solenoid is just a Cantor-continuum of circles, wired together in a particular way. This suggests to us the construction by [[symbolic dynamics]], where we start with a circle as a "racetrack", and append an "odometer" to keep track of which circle we are on.

Define <math>S = S^1 \times \prod_{k=1}^\infty \Z_{n_k}</math> as the solenoid. Next, define addition on the odometer <math>\Z \times \prod_{k=1}^\infty \Z_{n_k} \to \prod_{k=1}^\infty \Z_{n_k}</math>, in the same way as [[P-adic number|''p''-adic numbers]]. 
Next, define addition on the solenoid <math>+: \R \times S \to S</math> by<math display="block">r + (\theta, n) = ((r + \theta \mod 1), \lfloor r + \theta \rfloor + n) </math>The topology on the solenoid is generated by the basis containing the subsets <math>S' \times Z'_{(m_1, ..., m_k)} </math>, where <math>S' </math> is any open interval in <math>S^1 </math>, and <math> Z'_{(m_1, ..., m_k)} </math> is the set of all elements of <math> \prod_{k=1}^\infty \Z_{n_k}</math> starting with the initial segment <math>(m_1, ..., m_k) </math>.

== Pathological properties ==

Solenoids are [[compact space|compact]] [[metrizable space]]s that are [[connected space|connected]], but not [[locally connected]] or [[path connected]]. This is reflected in their [[pathological (mathematics)|pathological]] behavior with respect to various [[homology theories]], in contrast with the standard properties of homology for [[simplicial complex]]es. In [[Čech cohomology|Čech homology]], one can construct a non-exact [[long exact sequence|long homology sequence]] using a solenoid. In [[Steenrod]]-style homology theories,<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.encyclopediaofmath.org/index.php/Steenrod-Sitnikov_homology|title = Steenrod-Sitnikov homology - Encyclopedia of Mathematics}}</ref> the 0th homology group of a solenoid may have a fairly complicated structure, even though a solenoid is a connected space.
